purpose: Octreotide is used to treat conditions where your body makes too many certain hormones, such as acromegaly (too much growth hormone) or certain tumors in the gut that cause severe diarrhea and flushing. It can also help control bleeding from certain blood vessels in the stomach and esophagus. Doctors sometimes use it to reduce symptoms from rare hormone-producing tumors.
how_it_works: Your body naturally makes a hormone called somatostatin that slows down the release of other hormones. Octreotide works like a stronger, longer-lasting version of that natural hormone. By mimicking somatostatin, it tells your body to slow down or stop making too much of certain hormones or fluids that are causing your symptoms.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include nausea, stomach cramps, loose stools or diarrhea, gas, and bloating — especially when you first start using it. You may also notice pain or discomfort at the injection site. Some people develop gallstones over time, and the medication can affect your blood sugar levels, causing them to go too high or too low.
warnings: Tell your doctor if you have diabetes, because octreotide can change your blood sugar and you may need to adjust your diabetes medicines. Gallstones are a known risk with long-term use, so your doctor may monitor your gallbladder. This medicine can also affect your thyroid and heart rhythm, so let your doctor know about any heart conditions. Do not stop taking this medication without talking to your doctor first.
typical_dosing: The regular (short-acting) form is usually given as an injection under the skin (subcutaneous) or into a vein, typically 2 to 3 times a day. The long-acting form (Sandostatin LAR) is given as a deep muscle injection once every 4 weeks in a clinic. Your exact dose depends on your condition and how well you respond to treatment — your doctor will find the right dose for you.
